books.section: Topic 9.5 Migration and Immigration, 1980 to the Present
Prosperity and a New World Order (1988–2000)

options.misconception: Post-1965 immigration came mainly from Latin America and Asia, not Europe.
options.text: The return of large-scale immigration from Europe after 1965

options.misconception: No such ban existed; the 1965 act set limits, but immigration from Latin America grew anyway.
options.text: A federal law that barred immigration from Latin America

options.misconception: The border was never closed, and crossings continued through the 1990s.
options.text: The closing of the border with Mexico in the 1990s to all crossings
Immigration from Latin America and children born in the United States to immigrant parents

rationales.A: Background: after 1965, the main sources of immigration were Latin America and Asia.
rationales.B: Background: the 1965 act capped Western Hemisphere immigration for the first time, but the flow still grew.
rationales.C: Background: the southwest border stayed open to legal travel and trade through the 1990s.
rationales.D: Background: most post-1965 immigrants came from Latin America, and their U.S.-born children added to the Hispanic population. Both flows pushed the share upward.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who was arriving. Background: after 1965, most immigrants came from Latin America and Asia.
2. Ask what happened next. Background: their children, born in the United States, counted as Hispanic too.
3. Two flows together, new arrivals plus their children, explain steady growth over forty years.
4. Europe, a ban, and a closed border all contradict what the books say happened.
Remember: population growth comes from arrivals and from births, so check both.
